title: The Journeys of Paul the Apostle
intro: According to the Acts of the Apostles, Paul made three missionary journeys, which Acts arranges as three separate accounts, and then travelled to Rome for his appeal to Caesar. It has been estimated that the journeys recorded in Acts covered over 12,000 kilometres by land and over 8,000 kilometres by sea.
ending: According to the traditional account, Paul reached Rome c. 60 CE and spent two years under house arrest. Acts ends with him preaching there while awaiting trial and does not mention his death, which is believed to have come after the Great Fire of Rome in July 64 and before 68.

stops.text: According to Acts, the Antioch community commissioned Paul and Barnabas, and Barnabas led at first. The traditional and majority dating of the first journey is 46–49 CE, against a minority dating of after 37 CE.
stops.quote: The first journey, for which Paul and Barnabas were commissioned by the Antioch community, and led initially by Barnabas, took Barnabas and Paul from Antioch to Cyprus then into southern Asia Minor, and finally returning to Antioch.

stops.text: In Cyprus, according to Acts, Paul rebuked and blinded Elymas the magician, who had been criticising their teachings.
stops.quote: In Cyprus, Paul rebukes and blinds Elymas the magician who was criticizing their teachings.

stops.text: Paul and Barnabas sailed to Perga in Pamphylia. There John Mark left them and returned to Jerusalem.
stops.quote: They sailed to Perga in Pamphylia. John Mark left them and returned to Jerusalem.

stops.text: On the Sabbath Paul and Barnabas went to the synagogue, where the leaders invited them to speak.
stops.quote: Paul and Barnabas went on to Pisidian Antioch. On Sabbath they went to the synagogue. The leaders invited them to speak.

stops.text: The second journey began in late autumn 49 CE, after the Council of Jerusalem. At Antioch Paul and Barnabas argued over taking John Mark, and parted: Barnabas took John Mark, and Silas joined Paul.
stops.quote: Paul and his companion Barnabas stopped in Antioch where they had a sharp argument about taking John Mark with them on their trips.

stops.text: Paul and Silas visited Tarsus, Derbe and Lystra. At Lystra they met Timothy, a disciple who was spoken well of, and took him with them.
stops.quote: In Lystra, they met Timothy, a disciple who was spoken well of, and decided to take him with them.

stops.text: According to Acts, Paul cast a spirit of divination out of a servant girl. Her masters, who lost income from her soothsaying, seized Paul and Silas, and the two were put in jail.
stops.quote: In Philippi, Paul cast a spirit of divination out of a servant girl, whose masters were then unhappy about the loss of income her soothsaying provided. They seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the authorities and Paul and Silas were put in jail.

stops.text: Passing by Berea, Paul reached Athens, where he preached daily to the Jews and God-fearing Greeks in the synagogue and in the Agora. He was taken to the court of the Areopagus and preached to the elite there.
stops.quote: They continued traveling, going by Berea and then to Athens, where Paul daily preached to the Jews and God-fearing Greeks in the synagogue as well as to the Agora and was taken to the court of the Areopagus where he preached to the elite including the Greek intellectuals.

stops.text: Paul arrived at Corinth and founded the church there, staying 18 months. The stay is dated from the reference in Acts to the proconsul Gallio, and Priscilla and Aquila became his helpers there.
stops.quote: Around 50–51 AD Paul arrived at Corinth and founded the Church of Corinth, he stayed there for 18 months.

stops.text: According to Acts, Paul travelled through Galatia and Phrygia and then to Ephesus, staying almost three years. He left after a silversmith incited a crowd against his preaching and pro-Artemis riots broke out.
stops.quote: Paul then traveled to Ephesus, an important center of early Christianity, and stayed there for almost three years, probably working there as a tent maker, as he had done when he stayed in Corinth.

stops.text: Paul went through Macedonia into Achaea and stayed in Greece, probably at Corinth, for three months. Commentators generally agree he dictated the Epistle to the Romans in this period.
stops.quote: Paul went through Macedonia into Achaea and stayed in Greece, probably Corinth, for three months during 56–57 AD.

stops.text: Paul and his companions called at Troas on the way back to Jerusalem.
stops.quote: On their way back to Jerusalem, Paul and his companions visited other cities such as Philippi, Troas, Miletus, Rhodes, and Tyre.

stops.text: Paul and his companions called at Miletus on the way back to Jerusalem.
stops.quote: On their way back to Jerusalem, Paul and his companions visited other cities such as Philippi, Troas, Miletus, Rhodes, and Tyre.

stops.text: Paul and his companions visited Tyre on the way back to Jerusalem, before a stop at Caesarea.
stops.quote: On their way back to Jerusalem, Paul and his companions visited other cities such as Philippi, Troas, Miletus, Rhodes, and Tyre.

stops.text: Paul arrived with a collection of money for the local community, on what was his fifth and final visit. Acts says he was seized after Jews from Asia accused him of defiling the temple.
stops.quote: In 57 AD, upon completion of his third missionary journey, Paul arrived in Jerusalem for his fifth and final visit with a collection of money for the local community.

stops.text: After a plot against him, Paul was taken to Caesarea and held under guard in Herod's headquarters. He was held there for two years by Felix, and when Festus proposed a trial in Jerusalem he appealed to Caesar.
stops.quote: Paul was taken to Caesarea, where the governor ordered that he be kept under guard in Herod's headquarters.

stops.text: According to Acts, the ship was wrecked on Melita, identified with present-day Malta. The islanders showed Paul unusual kindness, and he was met there by Publius.
stops.quote: Acts recounts that on the way to Rome for his appeal as a Roman citizen to Caesar, Paul was shipwrecked on Melita, which is present-day Malta, where the islanders showed him "unusual kindness."

stops.text: After leaving Malta, Paul travelled towards Rome and passed through Syracuse, the first of three places on that route.
stops.quote: From Malta, he travelled to Rome via Syracuse, Rhegium, and Puteoli.

stops.text: Paul passed through Rhegium on his way from Malta to Rome, after Syracuse and before Puteoli.
stops.quote: From Malta, he travelled to Rome via Syracuse, Rhegium, and Puteoli.

stops.text: Paul's route from Malta to Rome ended with a stop at Puteoli, after Syracuse and Rhegium.
stops.quote: From Malta, he travelled to Rome via Syracuse, Rhegium, and Puteoli.

stops.text: Paul arrived in Rome and, according to the traditional account, spent two years under house arrest. Acts ends with him preaching there from his rented home while awaiting trial.
stops.quote: Paul finally arrived in Rome c. 60 AD, where he spent another two years under house arrest, according to the traditional account.

notes: The article dates AD/CE; dates here use CE. The article gives no years for the stops of the first journey except the leg's traditional dating (46–49 CE, minority dating after 37 CE), so all carry c. The third journey has no start year in the article: Ephesus is set 'before 56 CE' (year 55) only because Corinth is 56–57; Troas, Miletus and Tyre are c. 57 from the end date. The shipwreck, Syracuse, Rhegium and Puteoli are undated in the article and carry c. 60 from the arrival in Rome. The article's second-journey section says Paul left from Jerusalem but then has him stop at Antioch; the stop is placed at Antioch. Ephesus also appears at the end of the Corinth interval (52 CE, with Priscilla and Aquila); it is left out of leg 2 and used once, for the third journey. Philippi, Rhodes, Berea, Derbe, Tarsus and the 52 CE stops (Cenchreae, Caesarea, Antioch) were left out for length, as was Damascus (before the journeys) and the conjectured Spain journey. The 'wp' for Troas is Alexandria Troas, my identification, not the article's. The article says Corinth in 56-57 is only 'probably' the place. Corinth and Ephesus-adjacent places have no entry: places.tsv has only the region Corinthia, so Corinth is null. Caesarea is null because places.tsv has only other Caesareas. All details of the arrest, hearing and shipwreck come from Acts as the article reports it. The Caesarea stop's two years under Felix follow the article.
